sundar.31.cau1: When I took my leave, she gave me her crest-jewel. Śrī Rāma received it and held it to his heart. My Lord, with both her eyes full of tears, the daughter of Janaka spoke a few words.
sundar.31.cau2: Clasp the feet of the Lord and his younger brother. O friend of the lowly, you who take away the distress of those who bow to you: in mind, deed and word I love your feet; what offence of mine, my Lord, has made you abandon me?
sundar.31.cau3: One fault of mine I admit: when I was parted from you, my life did not leave me. But the offence, my Lord, lies with my eyes: they stubbornly stop my life as it tries to go out.
sundar.31.cau4: Separation is a fire, my body is cotton and my breath is the wind: the body would burn up in a moment. But my eyes, for their own sake, keep shedding tears, so the fire of separation cannot burn my body.
sundar.31.cau5: Sītā's suffering is immense; O you who are compassionate to the lowly, it is better left untold.
sundar.31.do31: O treasury of compassion, every single moment passes for her like an aeon. Set out quickly, my Lord, conquer the host of the wicked by the strength of your arms, and bring her back.
sundar.32.cau1: Hearing of Sītā's grief, the Lord, the abode of bliss, felt his lotus eyes fill with tears: Can anyone who in word, body and mind has me for refuge meet with calamity even in a dream?
sundar.32.cau2: Hanumān said: My Lord, that alone is calamity, when one does not remember and worship you. What does the demon count for, my Lord? You will conquer the enemy and bring Sītā back.
sundar.32.cau3: Listen, Hanumān: among gods, men and sages, no one who wears a body has done me such a service as you. What can I do for you in return? My mind cannot even face you.
sundar.32.cau4: Listen, my son: I am not free of my debt to you; I have thought it over in my mind and seen that it is so. Again and again the protector of the gods gazes at Hanumān; his eyes brim with tears and his whole body thrills.
sundar.32.do32: Hearing the Lord's words and seeing his face and his body, Hanumān was overjoyed; overcome with love, he fell at his feet: Save me, save me, O Lord!
sundar.33.cau1: Again and again the Lord tries to raise him, but Hanumān, lost in love, has no wish to rise. The Lord's lotus hand rests on Hanumān's head: recalling that scene, Śiva, the lord of Gaurī, was rapt.
sundar.33.cau2: Then, steadying his mind, Śaṅkara went on with the most beautiful story. The Lord raised Hanumān, embraced him, and taking his hand seated him right beside himself.
sundar.33.cau3: Tell me, Hanumān: Laṅkā, guarded by Rāvaṇa, is a most formidable fortress; how did you burn it? Seeing that the Lord was pleased, Hanumān spoke these words, free of all pride.
sundar.33.cau4: The great prowess of a monkey is just this: he goes from one branch to another. That I leapt across the ocean and burnt the city of gold, slew hosts of demons and laid waste the grove,
sundar.33.cau5: All of that was your glorious power, O Lord of the Raghus; none of it, my Lord, was any greatness of mine.
sundar.33.do33: My Lord, nothing is out of reach for one to whom you are favourable. By your power, cotton can indeed burn up the fire beneath the ocean.
sundar.34.cau1: My Lord, be gracious and grant me devotion that never fails, which gives the greatest joy. Hearing Hanumān's utterly guileless words, Bhavānī, the Lord then said: So be it.
sundar.34.cau2: Umā, one who has come to know Śrī Rāma's nature cares for nothing but worship. Whoever takes this dialogue to heart has won devotion to the feet of Śrī Rāma.
sundar.34.cau3: Hearing the Lord's words, the hosts of monkeys cry: Glory, glory, glory to the compassionate Lord, the root of joy! Then Śrī Rāma summoned the monkey king Sugrīva and told him: Prepare to march.
sundar.34.cau4: Why should there be any delay now? Give the monkeys their orders at once. Seeing this wonder, the gods rained down flowers in plenty and, rejoicing, went from the sky to their homes.
sundar.34.do34: The king of the monkeys sent for them at once, and the troop leaders came in throngs: hosts of monkeys and bears of many colours and matchless strength.
sundar.35.cau1: They bow their heads at the lotus feet of the Lord; the mighty bears and monkeys roar. Śrī Rāma looked over the entire monkey army, turning his lotus eyes on it in grace.
sundar.35.cau2: Strengthened by Śrī Rāma's grace, the great monkeys seemed like mighty mountains that had grown wings. Then Śrī Rāma joyfully set out, and many fair and auspicious omens appeared.
sundar.35.cau3: For one whose glory is wholly auspicious, it is only the rule that good omens attend his setting out. Sītā learnt that the Lord had set out: her left limbs throbbed, as though telling her so.
sundar.35.cau4: Every good omen that came to Sītā was, for Rāvaṇa, an ill omen. The army marched; who could describe it to the end? Monkeys and bears beyond number roar.
sundar.35.cau5: Their nails are their weapons; bearing mountains and trees, they move as they please through the sky and over the earth. The bears and monkeys roar like lions; the elephants of the quarters stagger and trumpet.
sundar.35.cha1: The elephants of the quarters trumpet, the earth sways, the mountains rock and the oceans heave. The gandharvas, the gods, the sages, the nāgas and the kinnaras rejoice at heart; their sorrows are over. Fierce monkey warriors gnash their teeth, and many millions upon millions rush onward; with cries of glory to Śrī Rāma of mighty majesty they sing the many virtues of the Lord of Kosala.
sundar.35.cha2: Śeṣa, the noble lord of serpents, cannot bear the weight and swoons again and again; again and again he grips the hard back of the tortoise with his teeth. How fine he looks! It is as if, knowing Śrī Rāma's splendid march to be a most lovely setting-forth, the king of serpents were inscribing it, unfading and holy, on the tortoise's shell.
sundar.35.do35: In this way the Lord, the treasury of mercy, went and made camp on the shore of the ocean, and the many heroic bears and monkeys began to eat fruit here and there.
sundar.36.cau1: Over there, ever since Hanumān burnt Laṅkā and went away, the demons have lived in dread. In their homes they all think: there is no saving the race of demons.
sundar.36.cau2: When he whose messenger's strength is beyond description comes himself, what good can come to the city? Hearing the townspeople's talk from her messengers, Mandodarī grew all the more distressed.
sundar.36.cau3: In private, with joined palms, she fell at her husband's feet and spoke words steeped in wise counsel: My husband, give up your hostility to Śrī Hari; take to heart what I say, for it is greatly for your good.
sundar.36.cau4: His messenger's deeds, when they so much as think of them, make the demons' wives miscarry. Call your minister and send his wife back in the minister's care, my husband, if you wish for your own good.
sundar.36.cau5: To the lotus-forest of your race Sītā has come like a winter night, bringing it grief. Listen, my lord: unless you give Sītā back, not even Śambhu and Brahmā can do you any good.
sundar.36.do36: The arrows of Śrī Rāma are like a host of snakes, and the throng of demons like frogs. Before they swallow them up, give up your obstinacy and make some effort.
sundar.37.cau1: The wicked one heard her words, and he, notorious throughout the world for his arrogance, laughed: Truly, a woman's nature is timid; even in good times she is afraid; her heart is very faint.
sundar.37.cau2: If the monkey army comes, the poor demons will have something to eat and live on. That the wife of one at whose terror the guardians of the worlds tremble should be afraid is a great joke.
sundar.37.cau3: With these words he laughed, clasped her to his breast and went off to the assembly, his attachment grown all the greater. Mandodarī was anxious at heart, thinking that fate had turned against her husband.
sundar.37.cau4: As he sat in the assembly, news reached him that the whole army had come to the far shore of the ocean. He asked his ministers: Tell me what course is right. They all laughed: Just keep quiet.
sundar.37.cau5: When you conquered gods and demons it cost you no effort; what do men and monkeys count for?
sundar.37.do37: If minister, physician and guru, these three, speak pleasing words out of fear or hope, then kingdom, dharma and body, these three, soon perish.
sundar.38.cau1: Rāvaṇa had found just such helpers: they sing his praises, making sure he hears them. Seeing his opportunity, Vibhīṣaṇa came and laid his head at the feet of his brother.
sundar.38.cau2: Then, with another bow, he sat down in his own seat and, once given leave, spoke: Gracious one, since you have asked me for my counsel, I speak for your good, dear brother, as far as my understanding allows.
sundar.38.cau3: One who wishes for his own welfare, good fame, good sense, a happy destiny and joys of many kinds should turn away, my lord, from the forehead of another man's wife, as one turns away from the moon of the fourth day.
sundar.38.cau4: Though one be sole lord of the fourteen worlds, he does not last if he is at enmity with living beings. A man may be an ocean of virtues and accomplished, yet if he has even a little greed, no one calls him good.
sundar.38.do38: Desire, anger, pride and greed are all, my lord, paths to hell. Give them all up and worship Śrī Rāma, whom the saints worship.
